query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Using a liquid‐phase precursor method to synthesize nano‐sized ZrB2 powders, without introducing foreign secondary phases, can lower the preparation temperature below 2300 °C while yielding a more densely consolidated microstructure that reduces pore formation during long-term liquid plating exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2 ceramics produced at temperatures above 2300 °C with relatively coarse grains and inherent porosity that can lead to structural degradation during exposure to aggressive liquid plating baths.
generation.intervention: Employ a liquid‐precursor synthesis process to produce nano‐structured ZrB2 powders, which allows sintering at reduced temperatures.
generation.conditions: Preparation using the liquid‐precursor method at temperatures near 1200–1800 °C under an inert or controlled atmosphere, followed by consolidation into a dense ceramic body. Service conditions include prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath at operational temperatures relevant to the application.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale ZrB2 grains that promote enhanced diffusion and densification, minimizing the size and connectivity of pores.
generation.mechanism: The liquid‐precursor method creates a highly reactive, ultra-fine grain precursor that enables phase formation and densification at a significantly lower temperature compared to conventional powder synthesis. The reduced grain size and improved grain boundary diffusion minimize the formation of holes and defects that would otherwise coalesce during prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath.
generation.predicted_outcome: The nano-structured ZrB2 prepared via the liquid‐precursor method will exhibit a lower processing temperature, enhanced microstructural integrity, and reduced pore formation, leading to improved resistance to degradation during service compared with conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2.
generation.baseline: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 synthesized at >2300 °C, which typically has coarser grains and a more defective microstructure that is prone to pore formation and eventual component failure in corrosive service environments.
generation.boundary: Preparation boundary: sintering temperatures must be reduced to between 1200–1800 °C using the liquid precursor process without compromising single-phase purity. Service boundary: long-duration exposure to a liquid plating bath under realistic operating temperatures, where the ceramic’s structural integrity is critical.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain whether the liquid-phase precursor method used successfully for high-entropy ceramic powders can be directly adapted to single-phase ZrB2 without introducing secondary phases or adverse effects unique to the pure system. Additionally, scaling the nano-precursor synthesis to full dense ceramic components may present unforeseen challenges.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of ZrB2 ceramic samples: one using the conventional high-temperature (>2300 °C) process, and the other using the liquid-phase precursor method at 1200–1800 °C. After sintering, subject both sets to an identical long-duration immersion in a simulated liquid plating bath. Compare microstructural features such as grain size, density, and pore distribution, as well as mechanical integrity pre- and post-exposure.
measurements: X-ray diffraction to confirm phase purity
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for grain and pore analysis
Post-exposure analysis of surface integrity and pore coalescence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the liquid-precursor synthesized ZrB2 does not show statistically significant improvements in reduced processing temperature (i.e., sintering below 2300 °C), densification (lower porosity), and resistance to microstructural degradation after the plating bath exposure compared to the conventionally prepared ZrB2, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractA nano-dual-phase powder with ultra-fine grain size was synthesized by the liquid precursor method at 1200 °C. A series of single-phase high-entropy ceramic powders ((Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Mo)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta, Mo)B2) with high purity (C content less than 0.9 wt% and O content less than 0.7 wt%) and ultrafine (average grain sizes of 340–570 nm) were successfully synthesized at 1800 °C. The sample of (TiZrHfNbTa)B2 exhibited a hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure, and the metal elements were uniformly distributed at the nanoscale, microscale, and macroscale. This method did not apply to the preparation of all high-entropy ceramic powders and was unfavorable for the formation of single-phase high-entropy borides when the size difference factor exceeded 3.9%. The present work provides a guide for the development of ceramic-based composites through precursor impregnation pyrolysis.Keywords: liquid-phase precursor method, high-entropy diboride powders, solid solutions, microstructure, pyrolysis mechanism
